original_question: Let S be a finite simple group, and let G be a finite group for which there exists a bijection f: G → S such that |x| divides |f(x)| for all x ∈ G. Must G necessarily be simple?
target_in_paper: Problem 21.2 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)": let S be a finite simple group, and let G be a finite group for which there exists a bijection f:G→S such that |x| divides |f(x)| for all x∈G; must G necessarily be simple? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the official problem almost verbatim: it has S finite simple, G finite, a bijection f:G→S, the divisibility condition on element orders, and the conclusion asking whether G must be simple. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
missing_details: To make the question fully stand-alone, specify that |x| denotes the order of the element x. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
It is slightly clearer to say that f is a set-theoretic bijection, since no homomorphism property is assumed. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))

The official problem does not add any further hypotheses: S is simply a finite simple group as stated, and the question is whether this hypothesis alone forces G to be simple. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
refined_question: Let S be a finite simple group, and let G be a finite group. Suppose there exists a set-theoretic bijection f:G→S such that, for every x∈G, the order of x divides the order of f(x). Must G be simple?
justification: The draft is essentially the notebook’s official Problem 21.2, so the paper-faithful refinement should stay at exactly that scope rather than drift to broader recognizability-by-spectrum or same-order-type questions. The only useful sharpening is to unpack |x| as element order and to make explicit that f is merely a bijection of underlying sets. A nearby earlier problem, 18.1, asks the analogous divisibility-bijection question with a cyclic target, which confirms the intended meaning of the hypothesis but does not add extra assumptions to 21.2. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.0300.pdf))
